passage:
Subject: A plan so you can rest

Dear Devika,

Last night I saw you fall asleep at Amma's bedside with the phone in your hand. I have been thinking about it all day. For two months you have done every night and every visit, and I let it happen because you never complained. That was wrong of me.

One person cannot hold this up for the long run, so here is a plan. You take nights on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. I take the other nights and weekends. We hire a helper from ten to two on weekdays. And Thursday is your day off, no phone.

If it does not work, we change it. But please say yes.

Jasleen

qa.q: Which day is Devika's day off?
How does Jasleen feel about the past two months?
qa.a: Jasleen feels guilty and worried, admitting that letting Devika carry everything was wrong.

qa.q: What could Jasleen and Devika do if the hired helper does not suit Amma?
qa.a: They could try a different helper or change the hours, and adjust the rest of the schedule so nobody is overloaded.

qa.q: How might Devika feel reading the email?
qa.a: Devika may feel relief at the offer of rest but also some reluctance to let go, since Devika has held the whole load for two months.

grounding: The email shows a person who realises one sibling cannot carry everything and plans rest shifts, paid help for some hours and a day off.

passage:
Jatin, you asked how I've kept going for eight months with Amma's treatment. The honest answer: I nearly didn't. I'm Pranav, and for the first two months I did everything. Every hospital visit, every night shift, every pharmacy run, while working. In week nine I fell asleep at a traffic signal on my scooter. That scared me.
So I sat down and thought it through. This isn't a sprint; it's going to be a year at least. One person can't carry a year. So we made a plan. My sister takes Tuesday and Saturday nights. We hired a home nurse for four hours every afternoon. My cousin does the pharmacy on weekends. And I take one full day off every other Sunday: no hospital, no calls unless it's urgent.
I felt guilty on the first Sunday off. But I'm still here, Jatin. Amma needs me in month twelve too.

qa.a: At a traffic signal, on the scooter.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel on the first Sunday off?
qa.a: Pranav felt guilty taking the day off, even though it was part of the plan.

qa.q: Why does the shared plan make sense for a long illness?
qa.a: It spreads nights, pharmacy runs and afternoons across people and paid help, so no one burns out before the year is over.

qa.q: How might Pranav's sister experience the new plan?
qa.a: Pranav's sister takes on two nights a week, which is harder for her but likely feels fairer and keeps Pranav safe.

grounding: It shows someone realising one family member cannot carry a long illness alone and planning rest shifts, hired help and time off so the family can last.

passage:
Madhav sits at the desk next to mine, and for three months after his father fell ill he was the first in and the last out, then went straight to the hospital for the night. His eyes were red all the time. Once I found him asleep in the meeting room at lunch.
In June something changed. When I asked, he told me he had done the maths: "Papa's recovery will take a year. I can't do every night for a year. Nobody can." He and his brother had worked out a rota: alternate nights, a paid attendant for the afternoons, and one weekend a month when Madhav's aunt came from Indore so both brothers could rest.
I can't say how he feels about it inside. But he stopped falling asleep at his desk. Last week he went to a cousin's wedding and came back with photos.
— Nitin

qa.q: How long did Madhav say his father's recovery would take?
What might Madhav have been feeling in the first three months?
qa.a: He seemed exhausted and stretched thin, with red eyes and naps in the meeting room, though Nitin can't know his inner state.

qa.q: What else could support Madhav's plan over the year?
qa.a: Checking the rota every month and adding help if someone wears down, including someone to talk to about his own stress.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the change in Madhav?
qa.a: Nitin sees him rested enough to stop sleeping at his desk and even go to a wedding.

grounding: It shows a young man realising he cannot carry his father's care alone and planning alternate nights, paid help and rest weekends so the family can keep going.
